summary: Reviewed the DVPWA (aiohttp + aiopg + redis) Python web application: DAO layer, views/routes, auth utilities, middlewares, app bootstrap, Jinja2 templates and config. The application is intentionally vulnerable and overall risk is critical: it contains an unauthenticated SQL injection, stored XSS enabled by globally disabled autoescaping, disabled CSRF protection, weak unsalted MD5 password hashing, missing authorization on state-changing endpoints, and insecure session-cookie settings. Coverage focused on all Python source and the templates that render user-controlled data; static assets and vendored JS/CSS were not reviewed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
findings.description: The student name is concatenated into an INSERT statement using Python %-formatting instead of a parameterized query, so attacker-controlled text becomes part of the SQL. The sink is reachable without authentication: POST /students/ calls views.students (sqli/views.py:57) which passes the raw form field data['name'] straight to Student.create, and CSRF validation is disabled (sqli/app.py:27), so any anonymous HTTP client can inject SQL (e.g. a name of "x'); DROP TABLE students; --" or a sub-select to exfiltrate password hashes).
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  -> await cur.execute(q). Source: views.students POST -> Student.create(conn, data['name']).
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query exactly like the other DAO methods: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with string formatting.

findings.title: Global disabling of Jinja2 autoescaping enables stored XSS
findings.description: Jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False for all templates, so every {{ ... }} expression renders raw HTML. User-controlled values are rendered unescaped, producing stored XSS. For example an anonymous attacker can POST a review (POST /courses/{id}/review -> Review.create) whose review_text is later rendered verbatim at sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22; course title/description (course.jinja2:14-15) and student name (students.jinja2:16) are likewise unescaped. Because the session cookie is not HttpOnly (sqli/middlewares.py:20), injected script can steal session cookies.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli', 'templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sink example: course.jinja2:22 `{{ review.review_text }}` renders Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) input with no escaping.
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=True, or select_autoescape(['html','jinja2'])) and only mark explicitly trusted strings as safe.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled
findings.description: The csrf_middleware (which validates the per-session _csrf_token on POST requests, sqli/middlewares.py:26-38) is commented out of the middleware chain, so no CSRF token is ever checked even though templates still render one. All state-changing POST endpoints (create student, create course, create review, evaluate/assign marks, login) accept cross-site forged requests. Combined with the missing authorization and SQL injection, this lets a remote site trigger those actions in a victim's browser.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[ session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware ] -- the CSRF middleware is commented out while middlewares.py:26 defines a working csrf_middleware.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list and ensure every POST form includes and validates the _csrf_token.

findings.title: Weak unsalted MD5 password hashing in User.check_password
findings.description: Passwords are verified (and, per the fixtures, stored) as plain unsalted MD5 hashes. MD5 is fast and broken: stored hashes are trivially cracked with rainbow tables/GPU brute force, and the lack of a salt means identical passwords yield identical hashes. If the database is read (e.g. via the SQL injection above), all user passwords are effectively recoverable.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  (from hashlib import md5).
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash such as bcrypt/scrypt/argon2 (e.g. werkzeug.security.generate_password_hash / check_password_hash) and use a constant-time comparison.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (mark assignment, student/course/review creation)
findings.description: The evaluate handler assigns grades (Mark.create) but has no @authorize decorator and performs no permission check; only the UI hides the form behind auth_user.is_admin (sqli/templates/course.jinja2:41), which is not an access control. Any anonymous client can POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} to set marks. The same missing-authorization pattern applies to views.students POST (create student, line 54-57), views.courses POST (create course, line 86-90) and views.review POST (create review, line 119-129): all mutate data with no authentication or role check. Only logout is decorated with @authorize.
findings.evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']) -- no @authorize, no is_admin check; contrast with @authorize() on logout (views.py:156).
findings.recommendation: Apply the existing authorize() decorator (with ensure_admin=True where appropriate) to all state-changing handlers and verify the user's role server-side before mutating data.

findings.title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly flag
findings.description: The Redis-backed session storage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is exposed to client-side JavaScript. Together with the stored XSS from disabled autoescaping, an attacker's injected script can read document.cookie and hijack authenticated sessions. No Secure flag is set either, allowing transmission over plaintext HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Create the session storage with httponly=True (the default) and secure=True, and serve the app over HTTPS.

findings.title: aiohttp application runs with debug mode enabled
findings.description: The Application is constructed with debug=True, which enables verbose diagnostics and additional runtime checks that can leak internal details and degrade performance if deployed to production.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False for production deployments.
